html:
Sukhothai and Ayutthaya were the Thai kingdoms that ruled much of what is now Thailand from the 13th century to 1767. Sukhothai came first, from about 1238; Ayutthaya, founded in 1351, absorbed it and became one of the great powers of Asia.

Tai-speaking peoples had moved south from southern China into lands held by the Mon and the Khmer Empire. Around 1238 Thai lords threw off Khmer control at Sukhothai. Its best known king, Ramkhamhaeng, is credited with creating the Thai script in 1283 and with patronising Theravada Buddhism, though the inscription that says so has been debated.

Ayutthaya, on an island in the Chao Phraya River near the sea, grew rich from rice and trade:

  • It took Angkor in 1431 and absorbed Sukhothai during the 15th century.
  • European visitors in the early 16th century ranked it with Vijayanagara and Ming China as one of the three great powers of Asia.
  • Its port drew Chinese, Japanese, Persian, Portuguese and Dutch traders, including the Dutch East India Company.
  • Under King Narai (1657 to 1688) Persian and then French influence peaked, and an embassy went to Louis XIV in 1686.

Burma was its great rival. Ayutthaya was a vassal of Taungoo Burma from 1569 to 1584. In 1767 a Burmese army of the Konbaung dynasty took the city after a long siege and burned it. Within months the general Taksin drove the Burmese out and ruled from Thonburi, and in 1782 a new capital at Bangkok began the Chakri kingdom of Siam.
sum: Sukhothai and Ayutthaya were the Thai kingdoms that ruled much of what is now Thailand from the 13th century to 1767. Sukhothai came first, from about 1238; Ayutthaya, founded in 1351, absorbed it and became one of the great powers of Asia.
